
## Echinocandins · mechanism of action

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="55%"}
- Semisynthetic **lipopeptides**: a cyclic hexapeptide core with an N-linked acyl lipid side chain that is
  required for activity.
- They non-competitively inhibit **β-1,3-D-glucan synthase**, encoded by **FKS1** and **FKS2**, depleting
  β-1,3-D-glucan from the cell wall and causing osmotic lysis at the growing tip.
- The target has **no mammalian homologue** — the basis for the best safety profile of any antifungal class.
- Activity is **fungicidal against *Candida*** (apical lysis) but **fungistatic against *Aspergillus***, where
  the drug damages hyphal tips without killing the colony. Hence mould activity is reported as a **minimum
  effective concentration (MEC)**: the lowest concentration producing short, stubby, aberrantly branched hyphae.
:::
::: {.column width="45%"}
::: {.keypoint}
**Four agents, one spectrum.** Caspofungin, anidulafungin, micafungin and rezafungin differ substantially
in pharmacokinetics but have **similar spectra**, and guidelines treat the first three as interchangeable for
invasive candidiasis.
:::

::: {.pearl}
β-1,3-glucan is also the analyte in the serum **(1→3)-β-D-glucan assay**. Echinocandin exposure does not
reliably lower the assay result, and a rising BDG on echinocandin therapy should not be read as a
pharmacodynamic readout.
:::
:::
:::

## Echinocandins · microbiology and spectrum

| Organism | Typical MIC~90~ / MEC~90~ (mg/L) | Comment |
|---|---|---|
| *C. albicans* | 0.015–0.06 | Fungicidal; wild-type |
| *N. glabratus* (*C. glabrata*) | 0.03–0.12 | **First-line despite azole resistance**; FKS resistance up to ~10% at high-risk centres |
| *C. tropicalis* | 0.03–0.12 | Susceptible |
| ***C. parapsilosis*** | **0.5–2** | **Intrinsically elevated MIC** — naturally occurring **Fks1 P660A** substitution [@garciaeffron2008parapsilosis] |
| *P. kudriavzevii* (*C. krusei*) | 0.03–0.12 | Susceptible — important given intrinsic fluconazole resistance |
| *C. auris* | 0.06–0.25 | Active; **resistance ~3–5%** |
| *Aspergillus* spp. (MEC) | 0.015–0.06 | Active *in vitro*; **not monotherapy** |
| *Cryptococcus* spp. | >16 | **No activity** — glucan synthase not essential in the same way |
| Mucorales, *Fusarium*, *Scedosporium* | >16 | No activity |

::: {.caution}
**The two spectrum gaps that cause harm:** *Cryptococcus* (no activity at all) and *C. parapsilosis*
(elevated MICs — reconsider the echinocandin if the isolate is *C. parapsilosis* and the patient is not
improving).
:::

## Echinocandins · ADME {.smaller}

::: {.smaller-table}
| Parameter | Caspofungin | Anidulafungin | Micafungin | Rezafungin |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Oral bioavailability** | <10% | 2–7% | <10% | <10% |
| **Route** | IV once daily | IV once daily | IV once daily | **IV once weekly** |
| **Half-life (h)** | 9–11 | 24–26 | 11–17 | **>130** |
| **Protein binding (%)** | 96–97 | 84–99 | ≥99 | 97 |
| **C~max~ (mg/L), single dose** | 7.64 | 2.07–3.5 | 4.95 | 19.2 |
| **Steady-state AUC~0–24~ (mg·h/L)** | 87.9–114.8 | 42.3–53 | 111.3 | 827 |
| **Metabolism** | Slow peptide hydrolysis and N-acetylation; spontaneous degradation | **Not metabolised** — slow chemical degradation in plasma | Catechol-*O*-methyltransferase pathway | **Minimal** — most circulating and excreted drug is unchanged rezafungin |
| **Elimination** | 35% faeces, 41% urine | Primarily faeces, 1% urine | 40% faeces, <15% urine | 75% faeces, 25% urine |
| **Plasma clearance (mL/min)** | 10–12.5 | 16.67 | 10.5 | **3.1** |
| **Renal dose adjustment** | None | None | None | None |
| **Hepatic adjustment** | **Reduce to 35 mg/day for Child–Pugh 7–9** | None | None for Child–Pugh 7–9 | None |
:::

::: {.source}
Values as tabulated in the primary chapter source; rezafungin half-life and clearance confirmed in phase 1
studies [@sandison2017rezapk].
:::

## Echinocandins · distribution and the sanctuary-site problem

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="54%"}
- Echinocandins distribute **well into liver, spleen, lung and kidney**, where they accumulate and form
  **tissue reservoirs** from which active drug slowly returns to the circulation. Tissue persistence
  correlates with continued antifungal activity after plasma concentrations fall below the MIC.
- **High molecular weight and ≥96% protein binding block entry into urine, CSF, brain, prostate and
  (largely) ocular fluid** — anidulafungin CSF penetration is **<0.1%**.
- Despite low urinary concentrations, echinocandins have sterilised azole-resistant candiduria in case
  reports and work in experimental renal candidiasis — because they accumulate in **renal parenchyma** even
  though they do not appear in urine.
- A single dose of rezafungin achieved higher concentrations in intra-abdominal abscesses and liver at 48–72 h
  than daily micafungin in a murine model; clinical significance is unknown.
:::
::: {.column width="46%"}
::: {.caution}
**Do not use an echinocandin as sole therapy for:**

- *Candida* **meningitis** or any CNS candidiasis
- *Candida* **endophthalmitis** or chorioretinitis
- symptomatic *Candida* **cystitis** (urinary drug is negligible)
- **cryptococcosis** (no activity)
:::

::: {.pearl}
"Poor urinary concentration" and "ineffective in renal infection" are different statements. Parenchymal
kidney infection responds; luminal bladder infection does not.
:::
:::
:::

## Echinocandins · pharmacodynamics

- **Concentration-dependent killing** with a prolonged post-antifungal effect; efficacy tracks
  **C~max~/MIC** (or, equivalently in most models, AUC/MIC) [@andes2010echinopd].
- PD targets are **species-specific**: the free-drug AUC/MIC required for stasis is far higher for
  *C. parapsilosis* than for *C. albicans* or *N. glabratus* — pharmacodynamics, not just the MIC, explains the
  *C. parapsilosis* caveat [@andes2010echinopd].
- Front-loading is pharmacologically sound, and is the design principle behind **rezafungin**: population
  PK/PD modelling showed rezafungin attained stasis targets against all tested *N. glabratus* isolates from
  recent surveillance, where caspofungin, micafungin and anidulafungin failed at approved doses
  [@hoenigl2024novel].

::: {.caution}
**The paradoxical (Eagle) effect.** Growth resumes at concentrations well above the MIC *in vitro* for
*C. albicans* and others, mediated by cell-wall integrity and calcineurin signalling with compensatory chitin
synthesis [@wiederhold2007paradoxical]. It is a reproducible laboratory phenomenon whose clinical relevance
remains unproven — but it is the reason simply escalating the dose is not a reliable answer to echinocandin
failure.
:::

## Echinocandins · resistance

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="52%"}
- Resistance is conferred by mutations in **FKS1 and FKS2 hot-spot regions** (HS1, HS2), which reduce the
  sensitivity of glucan synthase to the drug by orders of magnitude [@perlin2015fks].
- **Rates:** uncommon overall, but may approach **10% among *N. glabratus*** at high-risk centres and is
  **3–5% in *C. auris***. Prior echinocandin exposure is the dominant risk factor.
- ***C. parapsilosis*** carries a **naturally occurring P660A** substitution in Fks1 — an intrinsic, not
  acquired, mechanism [@garciaeffron2008parapsilosis].
- *N. glabratus* can accumulate azole **and** echinocandin resistance, facilitated by a **mismatch-repair
  defect (mutator) phenotype** prevalent in clinical isolates.
:::
::: {.column width="48%"}
::: {.keypoint}
**FKS mutations predict failure better than MIC alone.** An isolate with a hot-spot mutation may test as
intermediate yet fail clinically. Where echinocandin failure occurs in *N. glabratus* or *C. auris*,
**sequence *FKS***, do not simply increase the dose.
:::

::: {.pearl}
Rezafungin resistance is also FKS-mediated and requires higher concentrations against HS1 mutants, exactly as
for the older agents. Whether weekly dosing with prolonged sub-MIC tails in colonising flora will **select** or
**suppress** resistance is a genuine open question.
:::
:::
:::

## Echinocandins · safety and interactions

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
**Adverse effects — the class is remarkably safe**

- Infusion-related histamine-mediated reactions (flushing, rash), usually rate-dependent.
- Transient transaminase elevation; clinically significant hepatotoxicity is rare.
- Fever, headache, phlebitis; hypokalaemia in trial populations is usually attributable to the underlying
  illness.
- **No renal dose adjustment** for any agent; **no nephrotoxicity**.
- Caspofungin requires dose reduction in moderate hepatic impairment; the others do not.
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
**Drug interactions — minimal and agent-specific**

| Interacting drug | Effect |
|---|---|
| Tacrolimus | Caspofungin reduces tacrolimus AUC and peak by ~20%; no effect with anidulafungin, micafungin or rezafungin |
| Ciclosporin | **Caspofungin AUC increases ~35%**; anidulafungin AUC increases 22%; ciclosporin clearance falls 16% with micafungin; no effect with rezafungin |
| Sirolimus | Sirolimus AUC increases 21% with micafungin |
| Nifedipine | AUC increases 18% with micafungin |
| Rifampicin | Reduces caspofungin steady-state concentrations — **increase caspofungin to 70 mg/day** |
| Voriconazole | No significant interaction |

Rezafungin showed no meaningful effect on probe substrates for CYP3A4, CYP2B6, CYP1A2, CYP2C8, P-gp, OATP,
BCRP or OCT/MATE transporters.
:::
:::

## Echinocandins · clinical use

| Indication | Evidence |
|---|---|
| **Candidaemia and invasive candidiasis — first line** | Caspofungin non-inferior (and better tolerated) than amphotericin B deoxycholate [@moraduarte2002caspo]; anidulafungin non-inferior to fluconazole [@reboli2007anidula]; micafungin non-inferior to liposomal amphotericin B [@kuse2007mica] and equivalent to caspofungin [@pappas2007mica] |
| **Empirical therapy in neutropenic fever** | Caspofungin and micafungin are established options |
| **Prophylaxis** | Micafungin in HSCT; echinocandins where azole interactions are prohibitive |
| **Invasive aspergillosis** | **Not monotherapy.** Salvage or combination use only [@patterson2016idsaaspergillosis] |
| **Oesophageal candidiasis** | Effective, but relapse is higher than with fluconazole; reserve for azole-resistant disease |

::: {.keypoint}
**Why echinocandins became first-line for candidaemia:** fungicidal activity, retained activity against
azole-resistant *N. glabratus* and *P. kudriavzevii*, an excellent safety profile, and almost no drug
interactions — accepting the trade-off of IV-only administration and no sanctuary-site penetration
[@pappas2016idsacandida].
:::
